entry.title: China's Star 50 Index Drops 40% Amid AI and Semiconductor Valuation Collapse
entry.content:
Links: reuters.com | hacker news

China's Star 50 index, which tracks leading artificial intelligence and semiconductor companies, has fallen 40 percent in less than four months from its July peak. The market downturn has erased approximately $480 billion in market value amid collapsing valuations.

The sharp decline reflects mounting investor concerns over waning artificial intelligence demand and the impact of strict export curbs on Chinese technology firms. Major industry players have experienced steep drops, including chipmaker CXMT, which declined roughly 25 percent in the past month.

entry.title: Flock CEO Garrett Langley Dismisses Backlash in Leaked Audio
entry.content:

Langley also stated that his wife advised him never to apologize for corporate mistakes and expressed a desire to avoid media interviews in the future.

Despite the mounting backlash, Langley maintained that the opposition will eventually subside as the industry moves past the current period of intense public debate.

entry.title: Elvis Presley Rightsholders Sue Anthropic Over Alleged Copyright Infringement
entry.content:
Links: nytimes.com

The owners of Elvis Presley's music catalog have filed a federal lawsuit seeking more than $41 million in damages against artificial intelligence company Anthropic. The complaint alleges that Anthropic used 274 copyrighted musical compositions associated with Presley to train its Claude AI models without authorization.

The lawsuit, brought by a subsidiary of Authentic Brands Group, claims the company infringed on intellectual property rights by training its systems on copyrighted lyrics and generating infringing outputs. Anthropic has stated that it disagrees with the allegations and intends to defend itself against the claims.

entry.title: Eugene Police Department Charges News Outlet $2.5 Million for Police Misconduct Records
entry.content:
Links: theintercept.com | source | hacker news

The Eugene Police Department in Oregon billed local news outlet Double Sided Media nearly $2.5 million to fulfill a public records request regarding misconduct by police officer Justin Peckels. A separate request for records concerning a former officer added another $195,000, bringing total fee estimates for the two inquiries to nearly $2.7 million.

The department justified the multimillion-dollar cost by claiming it was required to search all records across all city employees past and present, a tactic critics describe as an intentional effort to make requests prohibitively expensive. The case highlights broader transparency hurdles where exorbitant fees and software limitations are used to obstruct public oversight of law enforcement agencies.

entry.title: Missileer Watch Tracks Military Emergency Action Messages on Shortwave Radio
entry.content:
Links: missileer.watch | hacker news

Missileer Watch is an online platform that provides a live shortwave radio feed and historical archive of United States military Emergency Action Messages broadcast over the High Frequency Global Communications System on 11175 kHz. The site makes intercepted tactical broadcasts accessible to the public alongside crowd-corrected transcripts and aircraft tracking data.

Developed by former 321st Missile Squadron combat crew member Daniel Frenkel, the project offers transparency into military communication channels without compromising operational security, as the underlying tactical messages remain heavily encrypted. Operating with minimal tracking and open-source licensing, the platform serves as a resource for radio enthusiasts and researchers monitoring strategic command traffic.

entry.title: Sleeping Giants Brasil and CTRL+Z Submit New Evidence of Meta Electoral Bias to TSE
entry.content:

Sleeping Giants Brasil and advocacy group CTRL+Z have submitted new evidence to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court alleging that Meta continues to favor the presidential campaign of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro over that of incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The filing claims that search results, image rankings, hashtag ordering, and Meta AI features on Instagram and WhatsApp display systemic biases that disadvantage Lula while promoting Bolsonaro and linking the president to derogatory content.

The latest legal challenge follows an earlier electoral court order requiring Meta to ensure equal treatment for both candidates under threat of substantial daily fines, which justices have recently threatened to double amid ongoing compliance disputes. Alongside the court petition, the organizations held a public demonstration at Meta's São Paulo headquarters to demand greater transparency regarding algorithmic ranking criteria and artificial intelligence outputs during the presidential race.

entry.title: Privacy Risks of Sensitive Data in Application Log Files
entry.content:
Links: fireborn.mataroa.blog | discussion

Log files attached to software support requests and bug reports frequently contain unintended sensitive information, including screen text, private messages, account identifiers, and authentication tokens. Because applications often log extensive internal state and user interactions during debugging, diagnostic files can inadvertently expose confidential personal data.

Users are advised to treat diagnostic warnings seriously and avoid blindly sharing unfiltered log archives when reporting bugs. At the same time, software developers bear responsibility for adopting safe defaults—such as keeping diagnostic logging disabled by default—and implementing selective logging to minimize privacy risks.

entry.content:

Federal lawmakers in Canada are advancing Bill S-211 to establish a national framework restricting sports betting and online casino advertisements across broadcasts, social media, and athletic gear. The legislative push follows new research conducted during the 2026 NHL playoffs showing that viewers are exposed to two to three gambling messages every minute, alongside rising rates of problem gambling and gambling-related suicides.

While health organizations and addiction researchers support federal intervention to curb pervasive marketing, the Canadian Gaming Association and provincial governments in Ontario and Alberta oppose the national framework. If approved by the House of Commons standing committee, the bill could lead to stricter regulations, including time-of-day bans and restrictions on celebrity and athlete endorsements.

entry.title: Canadian Bill C-22 Lawful Access Legislation Faces Opposition in Senate
entry.content:
Links: eff.org | hacker news

Canada’s Parliament is advancing Bill C-22, also known as the Lawful Access Act, which has passed the House of Commons and is currently before the Senate. The legislation would grant the government sweeping powers to mandate surveillance features, require telecommunications companies and messaging apps to retain user metadata for up to a year, and potentially compromise encryption by allowing backdoor access for law enforcement.

Civil liberties groups, including the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and Citizen Lab, have criticized the bill for severe constitutional, cybersecurity, and cross-border data-sharing risks. Critics warn that the measure could allow foreign law enforcement agencies, such as those in the United States, to access Canadian user data without domestic court oversight, prompting intense pushback from privacy advocates and the technology sector.

entry.title: Keep Android Open Campaign Challenges Google's Android Developer Verification Policy
entry.content:
Links: keepandroidopen.org | hacker news

The Keep Android Open campaign opposes Google's policy requiring all Android app developers to centrally register and provide government-issued identification before their software can be installed on certified devices. The mandate affects all applications, including those distributed via alternative open-source platforms like F-Droid or sideloaded independently, by introducing mandatory identity checks and cryptographic signing verification.

Critics and civil rights organizations argue that the policy undermines Android's open ecosystem, threatens open-source distribution, and introduces severe hurdles for independent developers. While Google frames the requirements around malware prevention and platform security, opponents contend that mandatory identity collection creates censorship risks and disproportionately impacts privacy advocates, hobbyists, and users operating under restrictive regimes.

entry.content:
